subject: NovumCorp connectivity options: VPC peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN
messages:
From: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@novumcorp.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Cc: NetOps Team <netops@novumcorp.com>, security@novumcorp.com
Date: 2027-04-03T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: Private deploy connectivity — initial requirements

Thanks Kimberly — quick background and the ask.

We’re kicking off an evaluation for connecting Novum’s VPCs (us-west-2) to a Redwood Private deployment. Key constraints:
- Regulatory: traffic must not traverse the public internet where possible; we need auditability and stable egress IPs for allowlisting.
- IP space: our infra uses RFC1918 ranges that might overlap with vendor VPCs (we’ll include ranges in the attached PDF).
- Ops: limited NetOps headcount; we prefer a model with minimal ongoing BGP/route maintenance.
- Failover: we want predictable failover behavior across AZs/regions.

Can you outline the tradeoffs between VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN? Also include operational impacts (who touches BGP/routing, whether Azure/AWS cross-account work is needed), and any blunt recommendations for a first pilot.

Attachments: novum-requirements-20270401.pdf, novum-network-diagram-v2.png

— Alex

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@novumcorp.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Tessa Morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-04-03T12:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity — initial requirements

Alex — thanks for the clear brief and attachments, very helpful. High level summary up-front: PrivateLink gives the strongest tenant isolation and simplest allowlistable endpoints; peering is lower-latency for large egress flows but brittle with overlapping IPs; site-to-site VPN is the fastest to stand up but weaker on SLAs and harder to scale securely long-term.

Below are concise tradeoffs and the operational footprint for each option.

1) AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints)
- Security: traffic never traverses the public internet; we terminate at ENIs in your VPC (you control sg/route rules). Good for allowlisting and per-subnet control.
- IP overlap: PrivateLink avoids direct routing between VPC CIDRs so overlap is fine.
- Ops: lower ongoing routing complexity. Vendor exposes an NLB/ENI-backed service; customer creates VPC endpoint. No BGP required.
- Latency/throughput: small additional hop via AWS network — fine for typical LLM inference (tens-hundreds ms per request), but be mindful of sustained throughput and ENI/NLB limits.
- Failure modes: AWS handles regional failover for the interface endpoints; cross-account endpoint approval may be required.
- When to pick: compliance-sensitive workloads needing strict L7 controls, allowlisted IPs, and minimal NetOps lift.

2) VPC Peering
- Security: native routing between VPCs, no transit gateway costs if pairwise. Traffic stays in AWS backbone.
- IP overlap: not allowed — requires refactoring or NAT. That can be a showstopper.
- Ops: requires route table management and can get messy at scale (N^2 peering). If you control both VPCs it's straightforward; cross-account peering needs coordination.
- Latency/throughput: lowest latency and best for very high throughput streaming.
- Failure modes: peering is resilient but any misconfigured route or propagation issue can cause outages.
- When to pick: when you need lowest latency for heavy streaming and you control IP planning or have non-overlapping CIDRs.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec)
- Security: encrypts over internet; can be placed behind transit appliances for additional controls. Ideal for quick POC.
- IP overlap: can be addressed with NAT but adds complexity.
- Ops: fastest to provision (hours-days). Requires tunnel endpoints and monitoring; long-term SLAs depend on vendor and link type (managed VPN vs customer router).
- Latency/throughput: variable, depends on internet and tunnel throughput; less deterministic.
- Failure modes: tunnel flaps and internet degradation. Good to pair with a fallback path.
- When to pick: proof-of-concept or customers who cannot change cloud setup and need time to plan peering/PrivateLink.

Recommendation (pilot): If auditability and allowlistable stable endpoints matter most, run a PrivateLink pilot (single-service endpoint scoped to a narrow set of subnets). If Novum expects sustained high-throughput streaming at very low latency and can address IP overlap, consider peering for a later phase.

Next steps I propose:
- Tech deep-dive: 60m session with Novum NetOps + Redwood infra (Ben + Markus) to validate IP ranges and throughput targets.
- Pilot request form + small test harness (we’ll host a limited-capacity model behind an NLB). I’ll attach a one-page pilot MOP after the call.

Happy to iterate — Ben and Tessa, any additions on limits or operational checks?

— Kim

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity — initial requirements

Quick operational notes from infra:

- ENI/NLB quotas: with PrivateLink we need to validate ENI quotas in Novum account; if they’re low we’ll either request quota increase or use a shared NLB pattern.
- Throughput shaping: we'll instrument token-level metrics and throttle at the load-balancer if you’re sensitive to burst costs.
- IP allowlist: PrivateLink produces stable interface endpoint IPs within your subnet — combine with egress NAT for single public IP if a WAF requires it.
- Cross-region: if you plan multi-region failover, PrivateLink is regional; peering/transit options required for global footprint.

I’ll bring a sample MOP and a checklist for the deep-dive.

— Ben
